Silicon reacts violently with liquid water to release oxygen while carbon dissolves like table salt
questions.explanation: Despite sitting directly above one another in Group 14 and sharing the same $$\text{XO}_2$$ oxide ratio, $$\text{CO}_2$$ consists of discrete gas molecules while $$\text{SiO}_2$$ is a hard high-melting solid.

questions.prompt: What do the slippery gray graphite in a pencil lead and a transparent gemstone diamond have in common?
choices: Both are ionic salts formed by carbon paired with trace alkali metals
Both are composed exclusively of pure carbon atoms arranged differently
Both consist of tiny isolated carbon molecules drifting weakly together
Both contain equal ratios of carbon and silicon atoms locked in rings
questions.explanation: Graphite and diamond are both pure elemental carbon; their contrasting hardness, color, and conductivity arise solely from how their carbon atoms are bonded in space.

chunks.title: Catenation: Carbon's Molecular LEGO Superpower
chunks.content_markdown:
Carbon's talent for building sprawling biological skeletons has a special name: **catenation**—the ability of identical atoms of an element to bond covalently to one another in long chains, branched trees, and rings. Picture assembling towers out of crisp, tight-fitting plastic LEGO bricks versus soft, oversized foam blocks. Tight bricks lock firmly into towering arches without toppling; bulky foam blocks wobble and collapse after just a few pieces.

Because carbon sits in compact Period 2, two carbon nuclei can pull close enough to form an exceptionally strong $$\text{C–C}$$ single bond ($$347\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)—nearly matching the strength of $$\text{C–O}$$ or $$\text{C–H}$$ bonds. That means long carbon chains stay stable even in the presence of oxygen and water. Step down to silicon, and larger atoms sit farther apart, weakening the $$\text{Si–Si}$$ bond to about $$226\,\text{kJ/mol}$$—far weaker than a rock-solid $$\text{Si–O}$$ bond. Consequently, catenation plunges rapidly down Group 14 ($$\text{C} \gg \text{Si} > \text{Ge} \approx \text{Sn} \gg \text{Pb}$$).

questions.prompt: What does the term catenation describe in main-group chemistry?
choices: The tendency of a metal oxide to dissolve in both strong acids and strong bases
The reluctance of heavy Period 6 metals to share their outer $$6\text{s}^2$$ electron pair
The ability of atoms of the same element to link covalently into chains and rings
The electrostatic attraction between a dissolved cation and surrounding water molecules
questions.explanation: Catenation is self-linking: the bonding of atoms of the same element to one another via covalent bonds to form extended chains, branches, or rings.

questions.prompt: Why does catenation drop sharply as you move down Group 14 from carbon to silicon and germanium?
choices: Heavier Group 14 atoms lose their p orbitals and cannot form any covalent bonds
Growing atomic radii lengthen self-bonds, making $$\text{Si–Si}$$ and $$\text{Ge–Ge}$$ bonds much weaker than $$\text{C–C}$$
Carbon has lower electronegativity than lead and therefore repels oxygen atoms away
Silicon atoms carry too many lone pairs to bond to more than one neighbor
questions.explanation: As atomic radius increases down Group 14, orbital overlap decreases and element-element single bonds grow progressively longer and weaker, sharply reducing catenation.

chunks.title: Carbon's Allotropes: Networks, Sheets, and Soccer Balls
chunks.content_markdown:
Different structural forms of the same pure element in the same physical state are called **allotropes**, and carbon is the undisputed champion of allotropes. Start with **diamond**: every carbon atom shares four single bonds with four neighbors arranged symmetrically in three dimensions, creating a single continuous giant molecule called a **covalent network solid**. Because breaking or scratching diamond means snapping strong covalent $$\text{C–C}$$ bonds, diamond is extraordinarily hard, melts above $$3500\,^\circ\text{C}$$, and conducts no electricity because all four valence electrons are locked in place.

Now rearrange those exact same carbon atoms into **graphite**. Each carbon bonds to only *three* neighbors in flat hexagonal honeycomb sheets. Its fourth valence electron enters a $$2\text{p}$$ orbital standing upright above and below the sheet, blending with neighboring $$2\text{p}$$ orbitals into a free-flowing electron highway! That makes graphite black and electrically conductive, while weak attractions between stacked sheets let layers slide smoothly onto paper. Peel off a single atom-thick sheet and you get ultra-strong **graphene**; curl a sheet into a hollow 60-carbon soccer ball and you get a **fullerene** ($$\text{C}_{60}$$).

questions.prompt: Why does graphite conduct electricity along its flat layers while diamond is an electrical insulator?
choices: Graphite contains metallic sodium impurities between its sheets, whereas diamond stays chemically pure
Diamond forms discrete low-melting molecules, whereas graphite is a three-dimensional ionic salt
Diamond has only three valence electrons per carbon atom, leaving an empty orbital gap
Graphite has free-flowing electrons across overlapping $$2\text{p}$$ sheets, whereas diamond locks all four electrons
questions.explanation: In graphite, each carbon forms three in-plane bonds and contributes its fourth electron to a free-flowing $$2\text{p}$$ network that conducts electricity; diamond locks all four valence electrons into rigid tetrahedral single bonds.

questions.prompt: What makes diamond a covalent network solid rather than a molecular solid like $$\text{C}_{60}$$ fullerene?
choices: Diamond contains positively and negatively charged carbon ions packed in alternating rows
Diamond dissolves easily in organic solvents to produce isolated four-carbon rings
Diamond is stitched continuously throughout the entire crystal by strong covalent bonds
Diamond is held together solely by weak attractions between separate soccer-ball cages
questions.explanation: In a covalent network solid, covalent bonds extend continuously across the entire crystal lattice rather than ending at discrete finite molecules.

chunks.title: Why CO2 Is a Gas While Quartz Sand Is a Rock
chunks.content_markdown:
Now we can solve the $$\text{CO}_2$$ versus $$\text{SiO}_2$$ puzzle with one clean orbital insight! To build a double bond—like the two $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bonds in carbon dioxide ($$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$)—atoms form one head-on bond plus a second side-by-side bond (a **$$\pi$$ bond**) between parallel $$p$$ orbitals. Think of two people standing close enough to shake hands directly *and* touch shoulders side-by-side.

Because carbon and oxygen are both compact Period 2 atoms, their $$2\text{p}$$ orbitals sit close together and overlap side-by-side beautifully. That makes $$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$ rock-steady as tiny, self-contained molecules that barely tug on one another—so $$\text{CO}_2$$ floats away as a gas! Now swap in Period 3 silicon. Silicon's larger $$3\text{p}$$ orbitals sit too far from oxygen's compact $$2\text{p}$$ orbitals for good side-by-side $$\pi$$ overlap—like two people standing a yard apart who can barely touch fingertips. Instead of unstable $$\text{Si}=\text{O}$$ double bonds, each silicon forms *four* strong $$\text{Si–O}$$ single bonds to four oxygen bridges, locking into a giant 3D **covalent network solid**: quartz sand!

questions.prompt: Why does silicon dioxide ($$\text{SiO}_2$$) form a hard covalent network solid instead of discrete $$\text{O}=\text{Si}=\text{O}$$ gas molecules like $$\text{CO}_2$$?
choices: Silicon has too few valence electrons to share four electron pairs with oxygen atoms
Oxygen atoms have much lower electronegativity than silicon and cannot share electrons closely
Silicon's larger $$3\text{p}$$ orbitals form poor side-by-side $$\pi$$ bonds, favoring four $$\text{Si–O}$$ single bonds
Silicon experiences a strong Period 6 inert-pair effect that locks away two valence electrons
questions.explanation: Effective side-by-side $$\pi$$ overlap works well for compact Period 2 $$2\text{p}$$ orbitals (giving molecular $$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$), whereas larger silicon favors a 3D network of four strong $$\text{Si–O}$$ single bonds.

questions.prompt: In solid quartz ($$\text{SiO}_2$$), how many oxygen atoms are bonded directly around each silicon atom?
choices: Two oxygen atoms linked by strong double bonds
Three oxygen atoms arranged in flat sliding sheets
Six oxygen atoms forming an ionic octahedral salt
Four oxygen atoms linked by strong single bonds in a 3D network
questions.explanation: Each silicon atom in quartz forms four single $$\text{Si–O}$$ bonds to four bridging oxygen atoms (each shared between two silicons, preserving the $$1{:}2$$ overall ratio).

chunks.title: The Period 2 Multiple-Bond Rule Moves Next Door
chunks.content_markdown:
Look how gracefully atomic size unlocked all of Group 14. Carbon's compact Period 2 orbitals deliver rock-solid $$\text{C–C}$$ self-linking (**catenation**), an astonishing gallery of **allotropes** spanning 3D **covalent network solid** diamond, conductive layered graphite, graphene, and $$\text{C}_{60}$$ fullerenes, plus strong $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ double bonds that keep $$\text{CO}_2$$ gaseous. Just one row down, silicon's larger size weakens $$\text{Si–Si}$$ chains and shuts down stable $$\text{Si}=\text{O}$$ double bonds—building rocky quartz and the vast silicate minerals that make up over $$90\%$$ of Earth's crust.

Keep that side-by-side $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$-overlap rule right in your front pocket as we step one and two columns right into Groups 15 and 16. That exact same Period 2 versus Period 3 split explains why nitrogen and oxygen fill our sky as invisible multiple-bonded gases while phosphorus and sulfur beneath them assemble single-bonded solids!

questions.prompt: Which Group 14 trend correctly orders catenation ability from strongest to weakest?
choices: $$\text{Pb} > \text{Sn} > \text{Ge} > \text{Si} > \text{C}$$
$$\text{Si} > \text{C} > \text{Ge} > \text{Sn} > \text{Pb}$$
$$\text{C} \gg \text{Si} > \text{Ge} \approx \text{Sn} \gg \text{Pb}$$
$$\text{C} \approx \text{Si} \approx \text{Ge} \approx \text{Sn} \approx \text{Pb}$$
questions.explanation: Catenation is overwhelmingly strongest in compact carbon and falls rapidly down Group 14 as self-bond energies weaken with increasing atomic radius.

questions.prompt: Why are compounds containing $$\text{Si}=\text{Si}$$ double bonds far rarer and harder to isolate than carbon compounds containing $$\text{C}=\text{C}$$ double bonds?
choices: Silicon's larger $$3\text{p}$$ orbitals achieve much weaker side-by-side $$\pi$$ overlap than carbon's compact $$2\text{p}$$ orbitals
Silicon has only three valence electrons and therefore suffers from boron-like electron deficiency
Silicon forms strictly ionic crystals whenever bonded to another silicon atom
Silicon atoms attract hydrogen so weakly that no silicon-hydrogen bonds can ever form
questions.explanation: Just as in $$\text{SiO}_2$$, the longer distance between larger silicon atoms prevents strong side-by-side $$3\text{p}\text{–}3\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ overlap, making $$\text{Si}=\text{Si}$$ double bonds far less stable than $$\text{C}=\text{C}$$.

sections.title: 8. Groups 15 & 16: Compact Multiple Bonds, Ring Allotropes & Hydride Quirks
sections.summary: Compares the pnictogens (Group 15) and chalcogens (Group 16) to show why compact $$\text{N}_2$$ and $$\text{O}_2$$ form gaseous multiple bonds while heavier phosphorus and sulfur build $$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedra and $$\text{S}_8$$ rings, alongside how hydrogen bonding elevates $$\text{NH}_3$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ boiling points while weaker bonds make heavier hydrides more acidic.

chunks.title: Invisible Air Above, Waxy Fire and Brimstone Below
chunks.content_markdown:
Take a slow breath in. Almost $$99\%$$ of the invisible gas entering your lungs comes from the top boxes of just two neighboring columns: nitrogen ($$\text{N}_2$$) from Group 15—formally named the **pnictogens (Group 15)**, from a Greek root meaning 'to choke', honoring nitrogen's inability to support breathing on its own—and oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) from Group 16, the chalcogens you met in Part I.

Now glance just one row down in those very same two columns. Directly beneath calm, unreactive nitrogen gas sits phosphorus, whose white allotrope is a waxy solid so reactive it bursts into flames spontaneously in open air and must be stored underwater! Directly beneath breathable oxygen gas sits sulfur, forming brittle lemon-yellow crystals around volcanic vents. How can two vertical pairs with identical valence-electron counts—five for Group 15, six for Group 16—look and behave like creatures from different planets?

questions.prompt: Which family of elements on the periodic table is formally called the pnictogens?
choices: Group 14 elements headed by carbon and silicon
Group 15 elements headed by nitrogen and phosphorus
Group 16 elements headed by oxygen and sulfur
Group 17 elements headed by fluorine and chlorine
questions.explanation: Group 15 ($$\text{N}$$, $$\text{P}$$, $$\text{As}$$, $$\text{Sb}$$, $$\text{Bi}$$) is known as the pnictogens, sitting between Group 14 and Group 16 (the chalcogens).

questions.prompt: How do the standard room-temperature forms of Period 2 nitrogen and oxygen contrast with Period 3 phosphorus and sulfur directly beneath them?
choices: Nitrogen and oxygen are diatomic gases, whereas phosphorus and sulfur are multi-atom solids
Nitrogen and oxygen are shiny metals, whereas phosphorus and sulfur are unreactive noble gases
Nitrogen and oxygen form yellow crystals, whereas phosphorus and sulfur are colorless liquids
Nitrogen and oxygen are ionic salts, whereas phosphorus and sulfur form isolated single atoms
questions.explanation: At room temperature, $$\text{N}_2$$ and $$\text{O}_2$$ are discrete diatomic gases, while their heavier Group 15 and 16 neighbors phosphorus and sulfur exist as larger solid allotropes.

chunks.title: Triple Bonds on Top, Tetrahedra and Crowns Below
chunks.content_markdown:
Remember the Period 2 $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$-overlap rule from Section 7? Watch it work its magic a second time! Compact Period 2 nitrogen and oxygen get close enough for superb side-by-side $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ overlap. Nitrogen locks two atoms together with a triple bond ($$\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$$, an astonishing $$945\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), making atmospheric $$\text{N}_2$$ famously stubborn to break apart. Oxygen forms a crisp double bond ($$\text{O}=\text{O}$$), staying a nimble diatomic gas.

Drop down to Period 3 phosphorus and sulfur, and their larger $$3\text{p}$$ orbitals once again overlap poorly side-by-side. Unable to build stable $$\text{P}\equiv\text{P}$$ or $$\text{S}=\text{S}$$ multiple bonds at room temperature, phosphorus and sulfur satisfy their bonding needs with *single bonds* to multiple neighbors! White phosphorus forms tiny four-atom tetrahedral pyramids ($$\text{P}_4$$) whose cramped $$60^\circ$$ bond angles act like cocked mousetraps—explaining why white phosphorus ignites in air, while calmer red phosphorus opens those cages into linked chains. Sulfur links via single bonds into eight-atom puckered crown rings ($$\text{S}_8$$), making sulfur a solid crystal rather than a gas!

questions.prompt: Why does elemental phosphorus form $$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedra and chains instead of diatomic $$\text{P}_2$$ gas like $$\text{N}_2$$?
choices: Phosphorus has only three valence electrons and therefore forms boron-style banana bonds
Phosphorus atoms carry a $$+5$$ ionic charge that repels neighboring phosphorus nuclei
Larger $$3\text{p}$$ orbitals form poor $$\pi$$ overlap, so phosphorus prefers three single $$\text{P–P}$$ bonds per atom
Phosphorus cannot form covalent bonds without first reacting with atmospheric oxygen gas
questions.explanation: While compact nitrogen forms an ultra-strong $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ triple bond in $$\text{N}_2$$, larger phosphorus prefers three single bonds to three neighbors, assembling $$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedra or chains.

questions.prompt: Why is white phosphorus ($$\text{P}_4$$) dramatically more reactive and flammable than red phosphorus?
choices: White phosphorus contains reactive alkali-metal impurities trapped inside its crystal lattice
White phosphorus is made of small $$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedra with tightly strained $$60^\circ$$ bond angles
White phosphorus is held together by strong $$\text{P}\equiv\text{P}$$ triple bonds that explode on contact
Red phosphorus has no covalent bonds and consists of isolated unreactive phosphorus atoms
questions.explanation: The tiny $$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedron forces sharp, strained $$60^\circ$$ angles that pop open readily in air; linking those cages into red phosphorus chains relieves the strain and lowers reactivity.

chunks.title: Hydrogen Bonding: Why Water Refuses to Be a Gas
chunks.content_markdown:
Now pair Groups 15 and 16 with hydrogen and compare their boiling points: $$\text{NH}_3, \text{PH}_3, \text{AsH}_3, \text{SbH}_3$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{H}_2\text{S}, \text{H}_2\text{Se}, \text{H}_2\text{Te}$$. Normally, heavier molecules boil at higher temperatures because larger, squishier electron clouds create stronger temporary attractions between neighbors. Follow Group 16 upward from heavy $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$ ($$-2\,^\circ\text{C}$$) through $$\text{H}_2\text{Se}$$ ($$-41\,^\circ\text{C}$$) to $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$ ($$-60\,^\circ\text{C}$$), and the smooth trend predicts light water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) should boil around $$-80\,^\circ\text{C}$$—leaving Earth a dry, oceanless desert!

Instead, water boils at a whopping $$+100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ (and ammonia, $$\text{NH}_3$$, jumps well above $$\text{PH}_3$$). Thank **hydrogen bonding**! When hydrogen bonds to a tiny, intensely electronegative Period 2 atom ($$\text{N}$$, $$\text{O}$$, or $$\text{F}$$), the bond becomes fiercely polar, exposing hydrogen's partially positive proton. That positive hydrogen latches electrostatically onto a lone pair on a neighboring molecule—like tiny molecular Velcro strips that require huge extra heat to peel apart.

questions.prompt: Why does water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) have a vastly higher boiling point than heavier hydrogen sulfide ($$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$)?
choices: Water is an ionic salt lattice whereas $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$ consists of neutral covalent molecules
Water molecules are larger and heavier than $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$ molecules at room temperature
Water forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds between polar $$\text{O–H}$$ bonds and neighboring lone pairs
Sulfur atoms have higher electronegativity than oxygen and repel adjacent $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$ molecules
questions.explanation: Oxygen's small size and high electronegativity create strong hydrogen bonds between neighboring $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ molecules, dramatically elevating water's boiling point above $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$.

questions.prompt: Which three small, highly electronegative elements are famous for creating strong hydrogen bonding when covalently attached to hydrogen?
choices: Carbon, silicon, and phosphorus
Sulfur, chlorine, and bromine
Lithium, beryllium, and boron
Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine
questions.explanation: Strong hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen covalently bonded to a compact, very electronegative atom with lone pairs: specifically $$\text{N}$$, $$\text{O}$$, or $$\text{F}$$.

chunks.title: The Acidity Surprise: Why Rotten-Egg Gas Beats Water
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a wonderful twist that catches almost everyone off guard! In water, an acid is a molecule willing to donate a proton ($$\text{H}^+$$). Since oxygen ($$\chi = 3.44$$) is far more electronegative than sulfur ($$\chi = 2.58$$) or tellurium ($$\chi = 2.10$$), you might naturally guess that water's more polar $$\text{O–H}$$ bond makes $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ a stronger acid than foul-smelling hydrogen sulfide ($$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$) or $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$.

Experiment proves the exact reverse! **Down-group hydride acidity** climbs steeply down Group 16: $$\text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{H}_2\text{Se} < \text{H}_2\text{Te}$$. Why does electronegativity lose the vote down a vertical column? Because atomic size grows rapidly with each new electron shell! Calling the Group 16 element $$\text{E}$$, every $$\text{H–E}$$ bond stretches longer and weakens down the group: oxygen's tight $$\text{O–H}$$ bond ($$463\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) clings fiercely to hydrogen, whereas tellurium's floppy $$\text{Te–H}$$ bond ($$267\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) snaps easily to release a proton.

questions.prompt: How does the acidity of Group 16 hydrides change as you move down the column from $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ to $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$?
choices: Acidity decreases sharply down the group because oxygen is the most electronegative element in Group 16
Acidity stays completely constant down the group because every hydride contains exactly two hydrogen atoms
Acidity peaks at $$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$ and then drops to zero for $$\text{H}_2\text{Se}$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$
Acidity increases sharply down the group because longer $$\text{H–E}$$ bonds grow weaker and release $$\text{H}^+$$
questions.explanation: Down a group, increasing atomic radius rapidly weakens the $$\text{H–E}$$ covalent bond; that steep drop in bond strength outweighs electronegativity and drives acidity sharply upward.

questions.prompt: Which Group 16 hydride donates a proton ($$\text{H}^+$$) most easily in aqueous solution?
choices: $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$
$$\text{H}_2\text{Se}$$
$$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$
questions.explanation: Tellurium is the largest atom of the four, giving $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$ the longest, weakest $$\text{H–E}$$ bond and therefore the greatest ease of releasing a proton.

chunks.title: One Column Left to the Halogens
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause and appreciate how cleanly the **pnictogens (Group 15)** and chalcogens (Group 16) echo everything we learned in Group 14. At the top of each column, compact Period 2 orbitals create strong multiple bonds (gaseous $$\text{N}_2$$ and $$\text{O}_2$$) and intense **hydrogen bonding** (keeping $$\text{NH}_3$$ and life-giving $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ liquid at unexpectedly high temperatures). Move down to Period 3 and beyond, and larger atoms switch to single-bonded solid allotropes ($$\text{P}_4$$ tetrahedra and $$\text{S}_8$$ crowns) while stretched, weaker $$\text{H–E}$$ bonds drive steeper **down-group hydride acidity**.

Now take one more step right into Group 17—the halogens ($$\text{F}$$, $$\text{Cl}$$, $$\text{Br}$$, $$\text{I}$$). Just one electron shy of a full noble-gas shell, the halogens are chemistry's fiercest electron grabbers. Get ready to watch both **down-group hydride acidity** and Period 2's cramped-orbital quirk show up in spectacular style—including why fluorine gas is far deadlier than chlorine even though chlorine has a higher electron affinity!

questions.prompt: Why does elemental sulfur exist as $$\text{S}_8$$ rings at room temperature whereas oxygen right above it exists as diatomic $$\text{O}_2$$ gas?
choices: Sulfur has eight valence electrons and must bond to eight separate sulfur atoms at once
Oxygen forms strong $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ double bonds while larger sulfur prefers two single $$\text{S–S}$$ bonds in rings
Sulfur atoms cannot attract electrons strongly enough to form any covalent bonds in air
Oxygen undergoes strong hydrogen bonding with itself to stay as light diatomic pairs
questions.explanation: Compact Period 2 oxygen forms stable $$\text{O}=\text{O}$$ double bonds, whereas larger Period 3 sulfur has weak $$3\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ overlap and instead forms two single bonds per atom inside $$\text{S}_8$$ rings.

questions.prompt: Which property of ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) compared to phosphine ($$\text{PH}_3$$) is directly caused by hydrogen bonding?
choices: Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than heavier phosphine
Ammonia forms solid tetrahedral $$\text{N}_4$$ cages at room temperature
Ammonia is a stronger acid in water than heavier Group 15 hydrides
Ammonia has longer, weaker $$\text{N–H}$$ bonds than phosphine's $$\text{P–H}$$ bonds
questions.explanation: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding between $$\text{NH}_3$$ molecules raises ammonia's boiling point ($$-33\,^\circ\text{C}$$) well above that of heavier $$\text{PH}_3$$ ($$-88\,^\circ\text{C}$$).

sections.title: 9. Group 17 Halogens: Oxidizing Muscle, the Fluorine Anomaly & Interhalogens
sections.summary: Traces the halogens from gaseous $$\text{F}_2$$ and $$\text{Cl}_2$$ to liquid $$\text{Br}_2$$ and solid $$\text{I}_2$$, exploring halogen displacement, why cramped lone-pair repulsion weakens the $$\text{F}\text{–}\text{F}$$ bond to make fluorine the fiercest oxidizer despite chlorine's higher electron affinity, why $$\text{HF}$$ is a weak acid, and how halogens form interhalogens like $$\text{ClF}_3$$ and $$\text{IF}_7$$.

chunks.title: Gas, Liquid, and Purple Crystals in One Column
chunks.content_markdown:
Walk down Group 17—the halogens ($$\text{F}_2$$, $$\text{Cl}_2$$, $$\text{Br}_2$$, $$\text{I}_2$$)—at ordinary room temperature, and you witness something no other column on the periodic table offers: all three classic states of matter lined up in neat order! Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a yellow-green gas, bromine is a fuming reddish-brown liquid, and iodine forms shimmering violet-black crystals.

All four exist as nonpolar diatomic molecules ($$\text{X}_2$$), so why do their boiling points climb so dramatically down the column? Remember how polarizability grew with anion size in Fajans' rules! As you descend from tiny fluorine to hefty iodine, each molecule gains more electron shells, creating a much larger, squishier electron cloud. Larger clouds slosh temporarily to create stronger fleeting electrostatic attractions between neighboring molecules—known as **London dispersion forces**—gluing heavy $$\text{I}_2$$ molecules into a solid while light $$\text{F}_2$$ floats freely as a gas.

questions.prompt: Why do the Group 17 halogens shift from gases ($$\text{F}_2$$, $$\text{Cl}_2$$) to a liquid ($$\text{Br}_2$$) to a solid ($$\text{I}_2$$) at room temperature?
choices: Heavier halogens develop stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonds between adjacent atoms
Heavier halogens have larger, more polarizable electron clouds creating stronger London dispersion forces
Heavier halogens switch from neutral diatomic molecules to three-dimensional ionic crystals
Heavier halogens form triple covalent bonds that lock neighboring molecules into flat sheets
questions.explanation: As molecular size and electron count grow from $$\text{F}_2$$ to $$\text{I}_2$$, the electron cloud becomes more easily polarized, strengthening London dispersion attractions and raising melting and boiling points.

questions.prompt: Which halogen is the only nonmetallic element on the periodic table that exists as a liquid at standard room temperature?
choices: Fluorine ($$\text{F}_2$$)
Chlorine ($$\text{Cl}_2$$)
Bromine ($$\text{Br}_2$$)
Iodine ($$\text{I}_2$$)
questions.explanation: At room temperature, $$\text{F}_2$$ and $$\text{Cl}_2$$ are gases, $$\text{I}_2$$ is a solid, and reddish-brown $$\text{Br}_2$$ is a liquid.

chunks.title: Oxidizing Muscle and the Halogen Displacement Ladder
chunks.content_markdown:
With seven valence electrons ($$n\text{s}^2 n\text{p}^5$$), every halogen sits just one electron shy of a stable noble-gas shell. That makes the halogens aggressive **oxidizing agents**—substances that pull electrons away from other species (becoming negative $$\text{X}^-$$ halide ions themselves). Just like a sports ranking ladder, oxidizing power peaks at the top of Group 17 and drops steadily down the column: $$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$.

You can watch this pecking order live in a beaker through **halogen displacement**! Bubble greenish chlorine gas through a clear solution of potassium bromide (containing dissolved $$\text{Br}^-$$ ions). Because chlorine sits higher on the oxidizing ladder, $$\text{Cl}_2$$ snatches electrons right off $$\text{Br}^-$$, turning into colorless $$\text{Cl}^-$$ while freeing reddish-orange liquid $$\text{Br}_2$$. Try the reverse—adding bromine to sodium chloride water—and nothing happens! A higher halogen always displaces a lower halide ion from solution, never the other way around.

questions.prompt: What happens when aqueous bromine ($$\text{Br}_2$$) is mixed with a colorless solution of potassium iodide ($$\text{KI}$$)?
choices: Bromine oxidizes $$\text{I}^-$$ ions, displacing elemental iodine ($$\text{I}_2$$) and forming $$\text{Br}^-$$
Iodide ions oxidize $$\text{Br}_2$$ to produce positively charged $$\text{Br}^+$$ metal cations
No reaction occurs because iodine is a stronger oxidizing agent than bromine
Both halogens react with water to release solid metallic potassium crystals
questions.explanation: Because oxidizing power decreases down Group 17 ($$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$), bromine sits above iodine and readily displaces $$\text{I}_2$$ from $$\text{I}^-$$ solution.

questions.prompt: Which order ranks the four common halogens from strongest oxidizing agent to weakest oxidizing agent?
choices: $$\text{I}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{F}_2$$
$$\text{Cl}_2 > \text{F}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$
$$\text{F}_2 > \text{I}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2$$
$$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$
questions.explanation: Oxidizing strength declines steadily down Group 17 from fluorine (the fiercest oxidizer of all elements) to iodine.

chunks.title: The Fluorine Bond Anomaly and Weak Hydrofluoric Acid
chunks.content_markdown:
Wait a second—check your Part II memory! In Part II, you learned the Period 2 compact-shell anomaly: chlorine actually has a *more exothermic* electron affinity than fluorine! So if an isolated chlorine atom welcomes an extra electron more eagerly than a fluorine atom, why is $$\text{F}_2$$ by far the stronger oxidizing agent?

Two factors combine to give fluorine an unbeatable edge. First comes **lone-pair bond weakening ($$\text{F}_2$$ anomaly)**: each fluorine atom carries three lone pairs squeezed into a tiny $$n = 2$$ shell. When two fluorines join in $$\text{F–F}$$, those six cramped lone pairs repel one another fiercely, stretching and weakening the $$\text{F–F}$$ bond ($$158\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) far below $$\text{Cl–Cl}$$ ($$243\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)! Because $$\text{F}_2$$ splits apart with tiny effort—and because tiny $$\text{F}^-$$ then releases gigantic hydration enthalpy in water—fluorine's overall electron-grabbing drive crushes chlorine's. Meanwhile, Section 8's down-group hydride acidity rule explains why hydrofluoric acid ($$\text{HF}$$) is a surprisingly *weak* acid while $$\text{HCl}$$, $$\text{HBr}$$, and $$\text{HI}$$ are all strong acids: the tiny, rock-solid $$\text{H–F}$$ bond clings stubbornly to its proton!

questions.prompt: Why is the $$\text{F–F}$$ single bond unexpectedly weaker than the $$\text{Cl–Cl}$$ single bond?
choices: Fluorine atoms have larger radii than chlorine atoms and overlap poorly
Six lone pairs crammed onto two tiny Period 2 fluorine atoms strongly repel one another
Chlorine forms a double bond between atoms whereas fluorine forms a single bond
Fluorine suffers from the heavy-atom inert-pair effect that locks away its valence electrons
questions.explanation: In compact $$\text{F}_2$$, the three lone pairs on each small fluorine atom sit very close across the short bond and repel strongly, weakening the $$\text{F–F}$$ bond relative to $$\text{Cl–Cl}$$.

questions.prompt: Why is aqueous $$\text{HF}$$ a weak acid whereas $$\text{HCl}$$, $$\text{HBr}$$, and $$\text{HI}$$ are all strong acids?
choices: Fluorine has a lower electronegativity than chlorine, bromine, and iodine
Hydrogen fluoride forms an insoluble ionic crystal lattice that never enters water
The short, exceptionally strong $$\text{H–F}$$ bond resists breaking to release $$\text{H}^+$$ protons
Hydrogen fluoride molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with surrounding water molecules
questions.explanation: Consistent with down-group hydride acidity, compact fluorine forms an unusually strong $$\text{H–F}$$ bond (reinforced by strong hydrogen bonding), making $$\text{HF}$$ donate protons much less completely than $$\text{HCl}$$, $$\text{HBr}$$, or $$\text{HI}$$.

chunks.title: Halogens Pairing with Halogens: Interhalogen Compounds
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens when you mix two *different* halogens together? Rather than ignoring each other, they react directly to form **interhalogen compounds**—molecules built strictly from two different halogen elements in neat odd-numbered ratios: $$\text{XY}$$, $$\text{XY}_3$$, $$\text{XY}_5$$, and $$\text{XY}_7$$ (such as $$\text{ICl}$$, $$\text{ClF}_3$$, $$\text{BrF}_5$$, and $$\text{IF}_7$$).

Look closely at which halogen sits at the center of the molecule: the *larger, less electronegative* halogen is always the central atom ($$\text{X}$$), surrounded by smaller, fiercely electronegative outer halogens ($$\text{Y}$$, most often fluorine). That makes physical sense—only a hefty central atom like iodine has enough elbow room around its waist to pack seven tiny fluorines into $$\text{IF}_7$$! And here is a wild twist: interhalogens are generally *more* reactive than pure halogens (except $$\text{F}_2$$ itself) because a polar $$\text{X–Y}$$ bond breaks more easily than a symmetric $$\text{X–X}$$ bond. Chlorine trifluoride ($$\text{ClF}_3$$), for instance, is so fiercely reactive it can set wet sand, concrete, and even laboratory glassware on fire!

questions.prompt: In an interhalogen compound of formula $$\text{XY}_5$$ (such as $$\text{BrF}_5$$ or $$\text{IF}_5$$), which halogen always occupies the central position?
choices: The larger, less electronegative halogen, because it provides room for smaller outer halogens
The smaller, more electronegative halogen, because it attracts electrons most strongly
Either halogen at random, because all halogens have identical covalent radii
Only fluorine, because Period 2 atoms can comfortably bind seven outer partners
questions.explanation: In interhalogens $$\text{XY}_n$$, the larger, less electronegative halogen serves as the central atom so more compact, highly electronegative outer halogens (especially $$\text{F}$$) can pack around it.

questions.prompt: Why can iodine form $$\text{IF}_7$$ whereas fluorine can never form $$\text{FI}_7$$?
choices: Iodine has more valence electrons than fluorine and needs seven more to reach an octet
Large iodine fits seven compact fluorines, while tiny fluorine lacks both space and bonding capacity
Fluorine cannot act as a central atom because it is strictly an ionic metal at room temperature
Iodine forms stronger hydrogen bonds with fluorine than fluorine can form with iodine
questions.explanation: Large iodine has both the physical room and available bonding capacity for seven tiny fluorines, whereas compact Period 2 fluorine is strictly limited by size and its small valence shell.

chunks.title: Standing at the Sealed Door of Group 18
chunks.content_markdown:
Look how every piece of Group 17 clicked together using the exact tools we have been building all along. Growing electron clouds turn gases into solids via London dispersion forces; top-to-bottom **oxidizing agent (halogen displacement)** ranks reactivity from $$\text{F}_2$$ down to $$\text{I}_2$$; **lone-pair bond weakening ($$\text{F}_2$$ anomaly)** plus massive $$\text{F}^-$$ hydration makes fluorine the undisputed champion oxidizer despite chlorine's higher electron affinity; and **interhalogen compounds** showcase fluorine's astonishing knack for wrapping around heavier atoms.

Now take the final step across the periodic table into Group 18—the noble gases. For over six decades, every chemistry textbook taught as ironclad law that noble gases could *never* form chemical compounds. Yet wait: we just met fluorine, the fiercest electron-grabber in nature, and from Part II we know ionization energy drops steadily down Group 18. Next, we watch a 29-year-old chemist shatter six decades of dogma on a single Friday night in 1962!

questions.prompt: Which pair of factors explains why $$\text{F}_2$$ is a stronger aqueous oxidizing agent than $$\text{Cl}_2$$ even though chlorine has a more exothermic electron affinity?
choices: Fluorine's higher boiling point and its ability to form seven-coordinate interhalogen cages
Chlorine's inert-pair effect and its refusal to dissolve in liquid water at room temperature
Fluorine's metallic conductivity and its tendency to form interstitial hydrides with oxygen
Fluorine's weak $$\text{F–F}$$ bond and the huge hydration enthalpy of tiny $$\text{F}^-$$
questions.explanation: Breaking the repulsion-weakened $$\text{F–F}$$ bond costs very little energy, and hydrating tiny $$\text{F}^-$$ releases enormous energy—together outweighing chlorine's slightly larger electron affinity.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly pairs a Group 17 compound with its expected chemical behavior?
choices: $$\text{HI}$$ is a much weaker acid than $$\text{HF}$$ because iodine is larger than fluorine
$$\text{I}_2$$ readily displaces $$\text{Cl}_2$$ gas when added to aqueous sodium chloride
$$\text{ClF}_3$$ is an intensely reactive interhalogen with larger chlorine at the center
$$\text{F}_2$$ has a much stronger single bond than $$\text{Cl}_2$$ due to tiny atomic size
questions.explanation: $$\text{ClF}_3$$ is a classic fiercely reactive interhalogen with larger, less electronegative chlorine surrounded by three small fluorine atoms.

sections.title: 10. Breaking the Noble-Gas Myth: Bartlett's Xenon Fluorides & VSEPR Shapes
sections.summary: Reconstructs Neil Bartlett's 1962 breakthrough comparing the nearly identical ionization energies of $$\text{O}_2$$ and $$\text{Xe}$$ to synthesize $$\text{Xe}^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$$, then applies intuitive VSEPR electron-pair repulsion to reveal why $$\text{XeF}_2$$ is linear, $$\text{XeF}_4$$ is square planar, and $$\text{XeF}_6$$ forms a distorted octahedron.
introduced_terms: xenon fluoride geometries (linear, square planar, distorted octahedral)

chunks.title: The 1962 Lecture Prep That Broke a Textbook Law
chunks.content_markdown:
For more than sixty years after the noble gases (Group 18) were discovered in the 1890s, every textbook called them the 'inert gases.' Their completely filled $$n\text{s}^2 n\text{p}^6$$ outer shells seemed like locked bank vaults—immune to every chemical reagent on Earth. Then, in early 1962, a 29-year-old British chemist at the University of British Columbia named Neil Bartlett spotted a number on a periodic-trend chart that stopped him cold.

Bartlett had recently discovered that deep-red platinum hexafluoride gas ($$\text{PtF}_6$$) was so fiercely oxidizing that it ripped an electron straight off ordinary oxygen gas ($$\text{O}_2$$), creating a crystalline salt, $$\text{O}_2^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$$. While preparing an undergraduate lecture, Bartlett checked the first ionization energies on a chart: stripping an electron from $$\text{O}_2$$ takes $$1175\,\text{kJ/mol}$$, whereas stripping an electron from heavy noble gas xenon ($$\text{Xe}$$) takes only $$1170\,\text{kJ/mol}$$—*slightly less*! If $$\text{PtF}_6$$ could crack open oxygen, Bartlett reasoned, it ought to crack open xenon too.

questions.prompt: What specific quantitative clue inspired Neil Bartlett to test whether xenon would react with $$\text{PtF}_6$$ in 1962?
choices: Xenon's atomic mass was nearly identical to the atomic mass of metallic platinum
Xenon's first ionization energy closely matched and fell slightly below that of $$\text{O}_2$$
Xenon's boiling point matched the melting point of liquid fluorine at room pressure
Xenon's electronegativity was higher than fluorine's on the Pauling scale
questions.explanation: Because $$\text{PtF}_6$$ had already oxidized $$\text{O}_2$$ ($$\text{IE}_1 = 1175\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), Bartlett realized it should also oxidize xenon ($$\text{IE}_1 = 1170\,\text{kJ/mol}$$).

questions.prompt: Why had chemists nicknamed Group 18 the 'inert gases' for over six decades prior to 1962?
choices: Their completely filled valence shells ($$n\text{s}^2 n\text{p}^6$$) were believed to prevent all chemical compound formation
Noble gases existed only inside stars and had never been collected in laboratory flasks
Noble gases reacted so explosively with air that no sample survived long enough to study
Noble gases carried zero protons and therefore could not exert any electrostatic pull
questions.explanation: Filled outer $$n\text{s}^2 n\text{p}^6$$ electron configurations (and $$1\text{s}^2$$ for helium) made Group 18 elements seem chemically unreactive under every ordinary condition.

chunks.title: Bartlett's Synthesis & Why Helium Still Refuses
chunks.content_markdown:
Working late on a Friday evening in March 1962—after his students had gone home—Bartlett broke the thin glass seal separating colorless xenon gas and red $$\text{PtF}_6$$ vapor. Instantly, a brilliant orange-yellow solid rained out of the gas! In a single dramatic moment, Bartlett had created the first true **noble-gas compound (Bartlett's synthesis)**, initially reported as $$\text{Xe}^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$$. The shockwave swept chemistry departments worldwide: within months, researchers at Argonne National Laboratory simply heated xenon with pure fluorine gas from Section 9 and isolated crisp, white crystals of xenon difluoride ($$\text{XeF}_2$$), xenon tetrafluoride ($$\text{XeF}_4$$), and xenon hexafluoride ($$\text{XeF}_6$$).

Why does xenon yield to fluorine while light noble gases like helium and neon still refuse? Check Part II's ionization-energy trend! Traveling down Group 18 adds electron shells and inner shielding, pushing xenon's outer $$5\text{p}$$ electrons far enough from the nucleus to lower its ionization energy dramatically—whereas tiny helium ($$2372\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) and neon ($$2081\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) lock their valence electrons far too tightly even for fluorine!

questions.prompt: Why does xenon form stable fluorides like $$\text{XeF}_2$$ and $$\text{XeF}_4$$ while helium and neon form no stable neutral fluorides?
choices: Helium and neon have lower ionization energies than xenon and evaporate before fluorine arrives
Xenon has only six valence electrons in Group 18, leaving two empty spaces for fluorine
Fluorine can only bond to radioactive elements located below Period 4 on the table
Xenon's outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus with more shielding, lowering its ionization energy
questions.explanation: Down Group 18, growing atomic size and inner-shell shielding sharply lower ionization energy, making heavy xenon far easier for fiercely electronegative fluorine to oxidize than compact helium or neon.

questions.prompt: Which three two-element xenon fluorides were rapidly synthesized after Bartlett's 1962 breakthrough by reacting xenon directly with fluorine gas?
choices: $$\text{XeF}$$, $$\text{XeF}_3$$, and $$\text{XeF}_5$$
$$\text{Xe}_2\text{F}$$, $$\text{Xe}_3\text{F}$$, and $$\text{Xe}_4\text{F}$$
$$\text{XeF}_2$$, $$\text{XeF}_4$$, and $$\text{XeF}_6$$
$$\text{XeF}_3$$, $$\text{XeF}_6$$, and $$\text{XeF}_8$$
questions.explanation: Heating xenon with increasing ratios of $$\text{F}_2$$ yields the famous even-numbered xenon fluoride trio: $$\text{XeF}_2$$, $$\text{XeF}_4$$, and $$\text{XeF}_6$$.

chunks.title: VSEPR Sculpting: Why XeF2 Is Linear and XeF4 Is Square Planar
chunks.content_markdown:
Holding real white crystals of $$\text{XeF}_2$$ and $$\text{XeF}_4$$ raised an irresistible 3D puzzle: how are the fluorine atoms arranged in space around xenon? Meet **VSEPR electron-pair repulsion** (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion)—really just Part II's Coulomb repulsion dressed up for 3D molecules! Picture tying inflated balloons together at their knots: electron groups around a central atom (both bonding pairs and unshared lone pairs) push one another as far apart as possible, and bulky lone pairs take up slightly *more* elbow room than tight bonding pairs.

Let us sculpt both shapes step by step. Neutral xenon starts with $$8$$ valence electrons. In $$\text{XeF}_2$$, xenon uses $$2$$ electrons for two $$\text{Xe–F}$$ bonds, leaving $$6$$ electrons as **3 lone pairs** ($$5$$ groups total → a 3D double-pyramid, or trigonal bipyramid). Putting all three roomy lone pairs around the wide middle 'equator' forces the two fluorines straight opposite each other into a **linear** ($$180^\circ$$) shape! In $$\text{XeF}_4$$, xenon forms four $$\text{Xe–F}$$ bonds and keeps **2 lone pairs** ($$6$$ groups total → an octahedron). Parking those two bulky lone pairs directly opposite each other (north and south poles) flattens all four fluorines neatly into a **square planar** shape!

questions.prompt: Using VSEPR electron-pair repulsion, how many lone pairs sit on xenon in $$\text{XeF}_2$$ and what molecular shape results?
choices: Zero lone pairs on xenon, producing a bent molecular shape
One lone pair on xenon, producing a trigonal pyramidal shape
Two lone pairs placed side-by-side, producing a tetrahedral shape
Three lone pairs around the middle belt, producing a linear shape
questions.explanation: Xenon's 8 valence electrons form 2 bonding pairs and 3 lone pairs (5 electron groups); the 3 bulky lone pairs occupy the spacious equatorial belt, forcing the two fluorines into a linear $$180^\circ$$ line.

questions.prompt: Why does $$\text{XeF}_4$$ adopt a flat square planar molecular geometry rather than a 3D tetrahedral shape like $$\text{CH}_4$$?
choices: Xenon carries two bulky lone pairs sitting opposite each other above and below the four fluorines
Fluorine atoms attract each other covalently to lock into a rigid four-cornered ring
Xenon lacks enough valence electrons to form four bonds without using $$3\text{c}\text{-}2\text{e}$$ bridges
Four fluorines are too small to repel each other in three dimensions around xenon
questions.explanation: In $$\text{XeF}_4$$, xenon has 4 bonding pairs plus 2 lone pairs (6 electron groups in an octahedral arrangement); placing the two bulky lone pairs $$180^\circ$$ apart leaves the four fluorines in a flat square planar ring.

chunks.title: The Wobbly Thumb: XeF6's Distorted Octahedron
chunks.content_markdown:
Now try the trickiest member of the trio: xenon hexafluoride, $$\text{XeF}_6$$! Count xenon's electrons carefully. Starting with $$8$$ valence electrons, xenon spends $$6$$ electrons forming six $$\text{Xe–F}$$ bonds, leaving exactly $$2$$ electrons—**1 lone pair**—for a crowded total of **7 electron groups** (6 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair).

If that lone pair sat quietly tucked inside a spherical $$s$$ orbital, $$\text{XeF}_6$$ would look like a perfectly symmetric six-cornered octahedron (like $$\text{SF}_6$$). Instead, gas-phase experiments reveal a delightful VSEPR twist: that lone pair is *stereochemically active*—meaning it pokes outward between the fluorines like an invisible thumb wedged into a crowded circle! Pushing the neighboring $$\text{Xe–F}$$ bonds slightly apart bends $$\text{XeF}_6$$ into a **distorted octahedral** shape that flexes fluidly as the lone pair wanders from face to face. Together, these **xenon fluoride geometries (linear, square planar, distorted octahedral)** turned once-'impossible' noble-gas compounds into VSEPR's greatest showcase.

questions.prompt: Why is $$\text{XeF}_6$$ a distorted octahedron rather than a perfectly symmetric octahedron?
choices: Xenon has only five valence electrons, leaving one outer fluorine atom weakly unbonded
Fluorine atoms repel each other into two separate $$\text{F}_3$$ triangles around xenon
Xenon's seventh electron group is an active lone pair pushing nearby bonds aside
Xenon's six bonds alternate between ionic fluoride salts and metallic bridges
questions.explanation: With 6 bonding pairs plus 1 active lone pair (7 total electron groups), the lone pair occupies space on one face of the octahedron and pushes adjacent $$\text{Xe–F}$$ bonds away, creating a distorted octahedron.

questions.prompt: Which list correctly matches $$\text{XeF}_2$$, $$\text{XeF}_4$$, and $$\text{XeF}_6$$ to their VSEPR molecular shapes in order?
choices: Bent, tetrahedral, perfect octahedral
Linear, square planar, distorted octahedral
Linear, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal
Trigonal planar, square planar, linear
questions.explanation: Counting lone pairs on xenon (3, 2, and 1 respectively) gives linear for $$\text{XeF}_2$$, square planar for $$\text{XeF}_4$$, and distorted octahedral for $$\text{XeF}_6$$.

chunks.title: The Main-Group Periodic Table, Unified from First Principles
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and admire the journey you just completed across the entire s- and p-block! We started with homeless hydrogen splitting into saline, covalent, and interstitial hydrides, watched lithium's hydration enthalpy and potassium's superoxide flip Group 1 expectations, and traced charge density across Group 2 into Fajans' diagonal twins ($$\text{Li}/\text{Mg}$$ and $$\text{Be}/\text{Al}$$). Crossing into the p-block, we saw boron invent $$3\text{c}\text{-}2\text{e}$$ banana bonds, heavy thallium and lead lock away their $$6\text{s}^2$$ inert pairs, compact carbon out-catenate silicon, nitrogen and oxygen out-$$\pi$$-bond phosphorus and sulfur, fluorine overcome its own cramped lone pairs, and Neil Bartlett's **noble-gas compound** crown it all with **VSEPR** **xenon fluoride geometries**.

Notice the quiet secret running through all ten sections: not a single 'exception' was truly random! Every twist flowed straight from Part II's toolkit—atomic size, effective nuclear pull, orbital overlap, and Coulomb repulsion. With the periodic table's main-group architecture now second nature, you are ready to step confidently into colorful d-block transition metals or 3D molecular chemistry!

questions.prompt: Which underlying periodic-table principle explains BOTH why xenon forms fluorides (while helium does not) AND why $$\text{H}_2\text{Te}$$ is more acidic than $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$?
choices: Increasing atomic size and shielding down a group weaken the nucleus's grip on outer electrons and elongate bonds
Decreasing atomic mass down a group makes heavier nuclei repel surrounding oxygen and fluorine atoms
Strong hydrogen bonding increases steadily down every column from Period 2 to Period 6
Relativistic contraction causes every Period 5 and Period 6 atom to shrink smaller than helium
questions.explanation: Descending a group adds electron shells and shielding: that lowers xenon's ionization energy enough for fluorine to oxidize it, and lengthens and weakens $$\text{H–E}$$ bonds to raise hydride acidity.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly links an iconic main-group phenomenon from this module to its root physical cause?
choices: $$\text{CO}_2$$ is gaseous while $$\text{SiO}_2$$ is solid quartz — caused by silicon's heavy-atom inert-pair effect
$$\text{PbO}_2$$ acts as a strong oxidizer — caused by the inert-pair effect stabilizing $$\text{Pb}^{2+}$$ over $$\text{Pb}^{4+}$$
$$\text{KO}_2$$ forms instead of $$\text{LiO}_2$$ — caused by potassium's higher hydration enthalpy in dry air
$$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$$ forms $$3\text{c}\text{-}2\text{e}$$ bonds — caused by hydrogen donating excess lone pairs to boron
questions.explanation: The inert-pair effect makes $$\text{Pb}^{2+}$$ much more stable than $$\text{Pb}^{4+}$$, giving $$\text{PbO}_2$$ strong oxidizing power; the other three choices mismatch their causes ($$\text{CO}_2/\text{SiO}_2$$ is $$2\text{p}$$ $$\pi$$ overlap, $$\text{KO}_2$$ is size-matched lattice packing, and $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$$ arises precisely because hydrogen has *no* lone pairs).
